name: Aisha Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, including what you say publicly and think privately. What is an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aisha, 27, and I lead four people checking small-business insurance claims; I have a bachelor's degree. I'm particularly good at spotting when a repair invoice covers damage from before the insured event, but our small insurer pays me near the bottom of the clerk scale. I use AI every day to draft requests for missing papers, with customer details removed and the wording checked. A completed claim is satisfying; an unanswered phone beside a queue of red reminders is less so.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the wage support outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent alone and have no children, with three weeks of expenses in savings after replacing a broken cooker. There are only two other insurance offices within a reasonable trip, and neither is advertising. I send my parents a birthday meal rather than money they need to live on. I favour earning your way and learning beside somebody who does the job; I also know my good work has not yet bought me a month's safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little help with letters is useful, but the insurer still has to explain why a claim was refused. A missing receipt is a question, not proof that somebody is lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage is low for this job and three weeks of cash goes quickly if the rent and electricity arrive together. I do not expect a great AI shake-up here, but I could lose paid hours if the office has a quiet month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking repair invoices and draft letters with the AI tool, removing personal details and checking every sentence. Starting now I'd stop the bought lunch twice a week and keep those spending cuts through the first year; the money stays available for that month's bills rather than becoming a promised savings payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills even when AI is modest. I can plan the next pay cycle, but I cannot pretend the fourth week of savings is already there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending change would you actually notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lunch is normally seven at the shop below our office, twice a week. I'd bring the rice and beans I already cook at home, not buy a new kitchen gadget to save on sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep checking yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still check that the invoice date fits the claim and call the customer if the papers disagree. Being quick does not give me permission to guess whether the leak happened before cover began.

say: I'd welcome **letter drafting** while explaining claim decisions properly.
I'd treat a **missing receipt** as a question, not proof of dishonesty.
think: My **three weeks saved** leave little room when household bills coincide.
I could lose **paid hours** in a quiet month despite modest AI change.
do: Keep **checking invoices** and AI-drafted letters after removing customer details.
Bring **lunch from home** twice weekly and keep the saved spending available for bills.
feel: **Anxious** about making low pay cover each bill.
S0.quote: A missing receipt is a question, not proof that somebody is lying.
fieldNote: Her **low lead pay** and thin savings matter more than the plateau's limited automation.
She distinguishes **lower spending** from committing money to a new savings deposit.

steps.text: Keep checking invoices and AI letters with customer details removed
Bring lunch from home twice weekly, leaving the spending difference available for bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster checking and replies might mean four clerks become three, rather than promise everyone an easier afternoon. I'd want to be judged on fair decisions, not how many letters a tool sends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink when software clears the ordinary paperwork. I use AI daily, but that does not mean the firm needs the same number of people checking its work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask our manager for one paid hour with the trainer to learn the new AI comparison tool on invented invoices. I'd complete the lesson only if the manager approves paid time, and otherwise keep our existing checks. Through the first year I'd also cancel my 18 monthly entertainment subscription so that bill no longer competes with electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, with enough control to ask for a real lesson and trim a real bill. I would not borrow for a badge that nobody at work uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be new about that lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current tool drafts words; the proposed one compares two versions of an invoice and flags changed items. I want to learn how to test a false flag, not let the flag become a refusal without checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid time is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the paid hour again at the next scheduled training review, but I would not practise on real customer papers at home. Cancelling the subscription is still within my control if the lesson is refused.

say: I'd expect **fewer clerk hours**, not automatically an easier afternoon.
I'd ask for **fair decisions**, rather than a target for letters sent.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink as routine paperwork moves to software.
My daily **AI use** does not guarantee the same staffing level.
do: Learn **invoice comparison** on invented papers only with manager-approved paid training time.
Cancel the **18 monthly subscription** through the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, able to request training and reduce one bill.
S1.quote: I would not borrow for a badge that nobody at work uses.
fieldNote: The **comparison lesson** adds a new skill beyond her existing daily letter drafting.
She keeps **paid-time approval** as a condition instead of funding unpaid home practice.

steps.text: Complete invoice-comparison training on invented papers only with manager-approved paid time
Cancel the 18 monthly entertainment subscription through the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that thinking AGI in 2028 could do our claim papers before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. I would not wait for a robot to walk into the insurance office before taking my wage seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to cut my post or most of my paid hours in that picture. Three weeks of cash and very few local insurance openings would leave me lying awake over rent, even if I am a good lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask my aunt Rosa whether she could offer a paid trial in her furniture-repair shop, with supervised work and no unpaid shift. I'd take a trial only if her actual written hours and pay cover my rent, bills and travel. If the insurance wage ends in the first year after 2028 without a suitable paid opening, I'd ask my parents for a specific month's rent, but count no help until they agree; I'd keep looking for paid vacancies if they cannot help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, waking up and calculating which week the rent falls due. I still have a plan to ask people, but no offer or family payment is in my account yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you actually do in your aunt’s shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa repairs chairs and cabinets herself, and I have only watched her on occasional visits. I'd start with supervised surface preparation, not claim that reading a claims estimate makes me a furniture restorer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How firm would the family help be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would need to check their own bills before saying yes to one month's rent. I would not tell the landlord that my parents had promised money when I had only asked, and their help would not create a permanent wage.

say: I'd expect **2028 thinking AGI** to reach insurance papers before 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd tell **my parents** that my wage could end.
think: I expect **major wage loss** despite being a capable team lead.
I would lie awake over rent with **three weeks saved** and few vacancies.
do: Ask for a **supervised paid trial** at my aunt's shop, accepting only written hours and pay covering rent, bills and travel.
Request **one month's rent** from my parents after 2028 wage loss only if no suitable opening exists; count only agreed help.
Keep **seeking paid vacancies** if my parents cannot help.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake over rent, without a confirmed offer or family payment.
S2.quote: I would not wait for a robot to walk into the insurance office before taking my wage seriously.
fieldNote: Her **expected wage loss** and sleepless rent calculations support alarm rather than merely possible disruption.
Both the **paid trial** and family contribution remain requests, with no assumed wage or gift.

steps.text: Take supervised paid trial only with written pay/hours covering rent, bills and travel
Ask parents for rent after 2028 wage loss without suitable vacancy; count only agreed help
Keep seeking paid vacancies if parental help is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until thinking AGI in 2031 is time to learn a practical repair task properly. Hands-on robots around 2034 mean a furniture workshop is a possible bridge, not an insurance policy against every later change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My insurance hours could still fall before the full 2031 system arrives. I have time to test whether I enjoy repair work, but I cannot pay for lessons by skipping rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the local repair college for a funded evening place in furniture surface repair, and enrol only if the fee is fully covered and the timetable leaves my paid insurance hours intact. I'd finish the supervised beginner term under those conditions; otherwise I stay at work and do not buy the course. In the first year after 2031, if my insurance pay falls, I'd apply to actual paid workshop openings only where written pay covers rent, bills and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not awake doing the same two-year sums. A funded term and a checked timetable are things I can find out about rather than wish into existence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before enrolment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the open evening I'd ask to see the workshop and the actual beginner tasks. Sanding a test panel under supervision is a more honest start than calling myself a cabinetmaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the insurance job while it pays and continue checking actual paid openings if hours fall after 2031. I would not drain three weeks of living money to make the college plan look definite.

say: I'd use **five years** to learn practical repair work properly.
I'd treat workshops as a **possible bridge**, with hands-on robots around 2034.
think: My **insurance hours** could shrink before full thinking AGI arrives.
I cannot fund **repair lessons** by missing rent.
do: Enrol in **surface-repair training** only with full fee funding and a timetable preserving paid insurance hours; otherwise keep working.
Apply after **2031 pay cuts** to actual workshop vacancies only where written wages cover rent, bills and travel.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to check funding and try a supervised beginner term.
S3.quote: Sanding a test panel under supervision is a more honest start than calling myself a cabinetmaker.
fieldNote: Her proposed **practical course** depends on funding and preserving her present wage.
The **2034 robot date** limits the imagined bridge without postponing the 2031 insurance exposure.

steps.text: Complete supervised repair term only with full fee funding and unchanged paid insurance hours
Seek workshops after 2031 pay cuts; require written wages covering rent, bills and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 is time to build a reserve before promising a different career. Insurance paperwork changes with thinking AGI then; later hands-on robots around 2039 do not keep my current desk busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The date is farther away, but low pay and three weeks of cash are still my life now. My hours could fall in an ordinary quiet month long before 2036, so I need a plan that starts with this year's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd put 20 monthly into a separate cash account only in months when rent, bills and food are paid, checking the balance each payday. If insurance pay ends in the first year after 2036, I'd apply for actual paid repair-shop vacancies with written wages covering my full rent, bills and travel. If no offer covers that budget, I'd keep searching rather than call an unpaid placement a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the next few years of pay, though the later date gives me more room to build money slowly. Twenty saved after the bills is better than a grand promise funded by an overdraft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a month with no spare 20?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would leave the 20 in the current account for that month's costs and try again next payday. Saving cannot come before eating or turn into a loan just to keep a chart rising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your aunt’s shop be your guaranteed next job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the actual written pay with the bills I have at the time, not today's rent carried forward for ten years. My aunt might have retired by then, so I would look for advertised openings rather than assume her shop was waiting.

say: I'd use the **decade** to build a reserve before promising another career.
I'd distinguish **2036 paperwork exposure** from later hands-on robots.
think: My **thin cushion** still matters to this year's bills.
I could lose **current hours** in an ordinary quiet month before 2036.
do: Save **20 monthly** only after rent, bills and food are covered; skip deposits in short months.
Seek **paid repair vacancies** after 2036 job loss, requiring written wages covering actual rent, bills and travel; otherwise keep searching.
feel: **Anxious** about current pay, with more time to build a reserve.
S4.quote: Twenty saved after the bills is better than a grand promise funded by an overdraft.
fieldNote: The later date does not remove **present low-pay pressure** or the risk of quiet-month hours cuts.
She refuses to assume her **aunt's shop** will still offer work in a decade.

steps.text: Save 20 monthly only after rent, bills and food; skip deposits in short months
Seek repair jobs after 2036 displacement; require written wages covering actual rent, bills and travel
Keep seeking paid openings if no repair offer covers the household budget

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect to lose most of my wage before I have a month's cushion. A real paid trial and clear notice from the insurer would help more than a certificate sold to frightened clerks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what being a lead pays in a small office. I can be the person everyone asks for help and still count the days until payday. Responsibility does not pay the electricity bill by itself.

headlineQuote: Responsibility does not pay the electricity bill by itself.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old claims lead** with a bachelor's degree, low pay and three weeks saved.
She **rents alone**, has no children and finds few similar local openings.
She uses **AI daily**, favouring paid practical learning and earning her way.
Her repair plans depend on **real wages** or funded study, never assumed family money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens most of her wage before she has a month's cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **real paid trial** and clear notice from her insurer would help.
